claim_1.claim: ELISA analysis of serum from 56 healthy volunteers showed anti-spike IgG binding antibodies increased after primary vaccination (day 0) and were significantly boosted after the secondary vaccination (day 21).

sources.quote: Primary vaccination induced binding antibody and neutralizing antibody responses in all but three individuals; these responses were boosted significantly after the secondary vaccination ( Fig. 1a , b , Extended Data Fig. 1b – d ).
Here we used systems tools to analyse immune responses in 56 volunteers ( Extended Data Table 1 ) who received two doses of BNT162b2 ( Extended Data Fig. 1a ).

claim_2.claim: Neutralizing Antibody Titer Assay analysis of serum from 56 healthy volunteers showed robust neutralizing antibody responses to wild-type SARS-CoV-2 after primary vaccination (day 0) that were significantly boosted after the secondary vaccination (day 21), declined about twofold by days 90–120, and in day-42 sera from 30 participants neutralization of B.1.351 was about tenfold lower than WA1/2020.

sources.quote: Primary vaccination induced binding antibody and neutralizing antibody responses in all but three individuals; these responses were boosted significantly after the secondary vaccination ( Fig. 1a , b , Extended Data Fig. 1b – d ).
The neutralizing antibody response reduced about 2-fold by days 90–120, this being comparable to the response to the Moderna mRNA-1273 vaccine 9 ( Fig. 1b , Extended Data Fig. 1c ).

BNT162b2 vaccination also induced a neutralizing antibody response against the B.1.351 variant of concern, albeit at a tenfold-lower magnitude than against the wild-type WA1/2020 (WA1) strain ( Fig. 1c , Extended Data Fig. 1f ), consistent with previous studies 11 .
Here we used systems tools to analyse immune responses in 56 volunteers ( Extended Data Table 1 ) who received two doses of BNT162b2 ( Extended Data Fig. 1a ).

claim_3.claim: Flow Cytometry analysis of PBMCs from 38 vaccinated individuals showed spike-specific polyfunctional CD4 and CD8 T cell responses were more readily detectable seven days after the secondary immunization (day 28) than at earlier timepoints, with CD4 responses primarily T-helper-1 type and IFNγ and TNF dominating CD8 responses.

sources.quote: Vaccination also stimulated spike-specific T cell responses, which were more readily detectable seven days after the secondary immunization ( Fig. 1d , e , Extended Data Fig. 2a – e ).
Consistent with previous studies 3 , the CD4 T cell responses were primarily of the T-helper-1 type, although there was a low-level T-helper-2 (IL-4) response ( Extended Data Fig. 2b ).

IFNγ and TNF were the dominant responses in CD8 T cells; three individuals with no known exposure to SARS-CoV-2 responded even at baseline, suggestive of CD8 T cells that are cross-reactive to related viruses, as has previously been shown 12 ( Extended Data Fig. 2d ).
Intracellular cytokine staining assay Antigen-specific T cell responses were measured using the intracellular cytokine staining assay as previously described 35 .

claim_4.claim: CyTOF analysis of whole blood from 27 individuals showed the frequency of intermediate monocytes (CD14 + CD16 + monocytes) increased significantly two days after the primary vaccination (day 2) and was substantially higher two days after the secondary vaccination (day 23), while pSTAT3 and pSTAT1 levels in multiple cell types were higher one day after secondary vaccination (day 22) than one day after primary vaccination (day 1).

sources.quote: We first assessed whole-blood samples of 27 individuals using cytometry by time of flight (CyTOF).

The frequency of intermediate monocytes (CD14 + CD16 + monocytes) increased significantly two days after the primary vaccination, and was substantially higher two days after the secondary vaccination ( Fig. 2b , Extended Data Figs. 5d , 6 ).
In addition, there were enhanced levels of phosphorylated (p)STAT3 and pSTAT1 in multiple cell types on day 1 after secondary vaccination, relative to day 1 after primary vaccination ( Fig. 2c , d ).

claim_5.claim: Olink analysis of plasma from 31 vaccinated individuals showed IFNγ and CXCL10 increased significantly on days 1 and 2 after primary vaccination (day 1 and day 2) versus baseline and increased further after the secondary immunization (day 21), with plasma IFNγ 11.3-fold higher at day 22 than day 1 and CXCL10 peaking at day 23.

sources.quote: To further investigate this phenomenon, we measured plasma cytokines in 31 vaccinated individuals using Olink ( https://www.olink.com/products/target/inflammation/ ).
Of the 67 cytokines detected, the concentration of 2 cytokines (IFNγ and CXCL10) were increased significantly on days 1 and 2 after primary vaccination ( Fig. 2e left).
Similar to our observations on intermediate monocytes and pSTAT1 and pSTAT3, the concentrations of these cytokines were increased even further after the secondary immunization ( Fig. 2e right).
The concentration of plasma IFNγ was 11.3-fold higher at day 22 relative to day 1 ( Fig. 2f ).
CXCL10 peaked on day 23 ( Extended Data Fig. 7a ).

claim_6.claim: RNA sequencing analysis of whole blood from 31 participants showed secondary vaccination (day 21) generated a greater transcriptional response than primary vaccination (day 0), with nearly a fourfold increase in differentially expressed genes at day 22 versus day 1, enrichment of antiviral and interferon response modules after both doses, and broader induction after the boost of dendritic cell activation, Toll-like receptor signalling, monocyte, and neutrophil modules on days 22 and 23.

sources.quote: Next, we performed bulk mRNA sequencing of whole blood from 31 participants.

Secondary vaccination generated a greater transcriptional response (as has previously been seen in a recent study of adjuvanted hepatitis B vaccine 17 ), with nearly a fourfold increase of differentially expressed genes at day 22 as compared to day 1 ( Fig. 3a ); this is consistent with the increased markers of innate immunity detected by both CyTOF and Olink ( Fig. 2 ).
Gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed that both doses of BNT162b2 stimulated antiviral and interferon response modules 18 ( Fig. 3b ).

In addition to the induction of antiviral pathways, secondary vaccination led to increases in signatures of dendritic cell activation and the upregulation of Toll-like receptor signalling, monocyte and neutrophil modules on days 22 and 23 ( Fig. 3b , Extended Data Fig. 8c , d ).

claim_7.claim: RNA sequencing analysis of PBMCs from 6 individuals by CITE-seq showed that one day after secondary vaccination (day 22) a myeloid cluster C8 expressing CD14, VCAN, CD1C, FCGR1A, CD274 and interferon-stimulated genes WARS, GBP1, IFI30 and IFITM3 emerged, increasing from about 0.01% of Lin − HLA-DR + cells on day 1 after primary vaccination (day 1) to about 1% after the boost, and this cluster showed higher IRF1, STAT1, STAT2, STAT3 and IRF8 with reduced FOS, JUNB, JUND and ATF3.

sources.quote: We performed cellular indexing of transcriptomes and epitopes by sequencing (CITE-seq) of 45 peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) samples from 6 individuals ( Extended Data Fig. 1a ) to disentangle these two effects and to examine transcriptional changes at the single-cell level.
Notably, cluster C8 (which expressed CD14 , VCAN , CD1C , FCGR1A and CD274 mRNA or protein) emerged on day 22, one day after secondary vaccination ( Fig. 4b ).

These cells uniquely expressed interferon-stimulated genes, including WARS (also known as WARS1 ), GBP1 , IFI30 and IFITM3 ( Extended Data Fig. 9d ), and constituted about 0.01% of the Lin − HLA-DR + population on day 1 after primary vaccination but increased almost 100-fold to about 1% one day after secondary vaccination ( Fig. 4c ).

C8 had a relatively higher expression of IRF1 , STAT1 , STAT2 , STAT3 and IRF8 and reduced levels of FOS , JUNB , JUND and ATF3 —the same transcription factors that defined the monocyte population in the previous study 25 ( Fig. 4g ).
